newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Normandy seen posting healthy profit.
newsitem.headline: Normandy seen posting healthy profit.

text.p: Australia's biggest gold miner, Normandy Mining Ltd, is expected to announce a healthy full-year profit this week as it eyes its October stock exchange listing in Canada and a possible shake-up of the Australian industry.

BZW's Barceps survey of 12 analysts showed an average forecast net profit before abnormals of A$120 million, with a range of A$113-126 million, for the first year after its merger with subsidiaries Posgold Ltd and Gold Mines of Kalgoorlie Ltd.
Normandy, which also now holds 75 percent of North Flinders Mining Ltd, posted net earnings of A$42.2 million in the year to June 30 96 prior to the merger's approval last August.
Normandy executive chairman Robert Champion de Crespigny, who has previously tipped record results for 1996/97, would not comment further ahead of their release on Wednesday.
But he told Reuters on Friday that having achieved critical mass, he aimed to lift earnings per share 10 percent a year.
"I want every single year from now on for us to do 10 percent and I know it will be cyclical but that is what we have got to do," he said.
With the Australian gold sector weakened by the gold price slump, De Crespigny said he expected and welcomed rationalisation but did not anticipate a much-touted "invasion" by North American miners.
"You will certainly have some foreigners coming, I think we should watch the South Africans, but you will also see mergers et cetera within Australia," he said.

Normandy has figured on both sides of ongoing speculation about takeovers, and De Crespigny said while the company would certainly pursue acquisition and joint venture opportunities, he also had no doubt Normandy's liquidity made it a target.
He said Normandy had received no formal offers, but would not comment on any indirect merger or acquistion approaches.

He ruled out a bid for rival Newcrest Mining Ltd, which holds an 11.8-percent stake in Normandy after an ill-fated move to join last year's merger process, but said clearly some of Newcrests' assets were of interest.

"Our own shares interest us, (Newcrest's 22-percent stake in the Western Australian gold mine) Boddington interests us," he said, acknowledging that the low gold price had cast a shadow over the proposed development of the Wandoo deposit at Boddington.

While the strong zinc price has helped the 1996/97 result, De Crespigny said Normandy's acquisition focus would be on gold but he ruled out any early disposal of the company's non-gold operations, although they remained under review.
"At some time it is possible we will do something with our base metals but we have no intention at the moment," he said.

De Crespigny did not want to comment publicly on a possible dispute with St Barbara Mines Ltd over the Cuddingwarra gold project in Western Australia, other than to say Normandy was keen to make the project "a harmonious joint venture".

As it looks also to a possible listing in the United States in late 1998, Normandy is undergoing a management restructure, with long-term operations chief Tony Palmer to leave and former Rio Tinto Ltd executive Ian Gould and John Fairfax Holdings Ltd's John Reynolds joining in strategic roles.

De Crespigny said while he hoped Palmer could be persuaded to remain in charge of Australian operations, Gould's appointment would allow him to focus more on strategy and political issues such as native title and the new gold royalty introduced in Western Australia state.

While he did not dispute the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) right to choose to sell 167 tonnes of gold as it has recently done, he said he remained concerned at imprudent statements by both the RBA and the government regarding the decision.

Outside Australia, Normandy's focus has come through its La Source venture with the French government's Bureau de Recherches Geologiques et Minieres (BRGM), which he said was now profitable, three years ahead of target.

Asked about possible changes by Paris to BRGM's structure and its ability to fund projects, he said Normandy was not seeking any change to a valuable relationship and had always been prepared where necessary to provide 100 percent of any project.

De Crespigny said there had been little advance in the legal dispute over the profitable Yanacocha gold mine in Peru with the Peruvian Compania de Minera Buenaventura SA and Newmont Mining Corp showing no interest in a settlement.
However, he was confident in the future of the Ovacik mine in Turkey despite local environmental opposition.
"In five years' time, we think La Source will be really hitting its straps...(and) hopefully by that time you will be starting to see Latin America emerge as a base for us," he said.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
